paragraphs.text: It was raining hard when Mina left the café. She took her umbrella from the stand by the door, opened it, and ran to the bus stop.
On the bus, she looked down at it and saw something strange. Her umbrella was black. This one was dark green.
"Oh no," she said. She had taken the wrong one.
She turned it around in her hands. It was old but good, the kind of umbrella you keep for years. Inside, a small piece of paper was taped to the handle. She pulled it off and read it.
If you found this, you have my umbrella. That's okay. Keep it. But please do one thing for me: be kind to someone today.
Mina laughed. Then she read it again and didn't laugh.
The bus stopped. An old man got on, wet from head to toe. There were no free seats. Mina stood up. "Here," she said. He smiled and sat down.
That's one,
she thought.
At work, her coworker Jun was at his desk with his head in his hands. Usually Mina walked past him. Today she stopped.
"Are you okay?"

He looked up, surprised. They talked for ten minutes. It turned out his mother was in the hospital, and he hadn't slept for two days. Before Mina went back to her desk, he said, "Thanks. Really. Nobody ever asks."
That evening the rain stopped, but Mina kept the green umbrella next to her bag. She didn't know why.

All week she kept counting. She held the door for a man with a heavy box. She called her sister, who she hadn't talked to since summer. On Friday she left work on time, bought herself a good dinner, and ate it slowly.

A week later, it was raining again. Mina went back to the same café. The stand by the door was full of umbrellas, and hers, the black one, was still there. She picked it up. Then she looked at the green one in her other hand.
She took a pen out of her bag, found a piece of paper, and wrote:
I had your umbrella for a week. I was kind to six people. One of them was me. Thank you. Now it's someone else's turn.
She taped the note to the handle, put the green umbrella back in the stand, and walked out into the rain with her own.
At the door she stopped and looked back. A young man in a hurry was reaching for the stand. His hand went past three black umbrellas and closed around the green one.
Mina smiled and opened her umbrella.

questions.question: Why did Mina have a green umbrella?
options: She bought a new one at the café.
She took the wrong umbrella by mistake.
A man on the bus gave it to her.
questions.explain: 카페 우산꽂이에서 자기 것인 줄 알고 집어 들었다. 버스에서 보니 검은색이 아니라 짙은 초록색이었다.

questions.question: What did the note ask her to do?
options: Bring the umbrella back to the café.
Call the owner of the umbrella.
Be kind to someone that day.
questions.explain: 쪽지는 우산은 가져도 된다며, 대신 오늘 누군가에게 친절해 달라고 했다.

questions.question: Why was Jun sitting with his head in his hands?
options: His mother was in the hospital and he hadn't slept.
He had a fight with Mina.
questions.explain: 어머니가 입원해 이틀 동안 잠을 못 잤다.

questions.question: "I was kind to six people. One of them was me." What does Mina mean?
options: She forgot to count one person.
She also took good care of herself that week.
She gave herself the green umbrella.
She was kind to the same person six times.
questions.explain: 금요일에 제때 퇴근해 자신에게 좋은 저녁을 사 주고 천천히 먹었다. 그것도 친절의 하나로 셌다.

questions.question: What happened at the very end?
options: The owner came back for the green umbrella.
A young man took the green umbrella with the new note.
Mina lost her black umbrella again.
questions.explain: 서두르던 젊은 남자가 검은 우산 셋을 지나쳐 초록 우산을 집었다. 이제 그 사람의 차례다.

questions.question: "Before Mina went back to her desk..." Why went, not came?
options: Her desk is far from the café.
The scene is at Jun's desk, and she moves away from there.
Went is the past tense of come.
Came would mean she never left her desk.
questions.explain: 장면의 기준점은 지금 이야기가 벌어지는 준의 자리다. 미나는 그 자리에서 멀어지므로 went back이다(go: 기준점에서 멀어진다).

questions.question: "His hand ... closed around the green one." What picture does this give?
options: His fingers wrapped around the handle and held it.
questions.explain: close는 열린 것이 닫히는 그림이다. 펼친 손이 손잡이를 감싸며 닫힌다. 그래서 '잡았다'보다 움직임이 보인다.
questions.basis: 모델 밖(작업자 판단). close는 표제어가 아니다

paragraphs.text: I drive the number 12 bus in a small city. I have seen a lot of strange things on my bus, but nothing like the dog.

He was brown, with one white ear. The first time, he got on at 7:15 at Hill Road, walked past me, and sat down by the window. Nobody was with him. I thought he was lost. But at Park Street, when the doors opened, he got up and got off like any other passenger.
At 5:30 that evening, he was waiting at Park Street. He got on, sat by the same window, and got off at Hill Road.
The next day he did the same thing. And the next. After two weeks, the regular passengers started saying good morning to him. A student named him Ticket, because he never had one.
"Where does he go every day?" people asked me. I didn't know. Nobody knew.
So on my day off, I found out.
At 7:15 I was standing at Hill Road in my own clothes. Ticket came around the corner, looked at me for a second, and got on the bus. I got on behind him. At Park Street we both got off.
He walked fast. He knew the way. Two streets, left at the bakery, then up a small hill. At the top there was a long white building with a garden. A sign on the gate said
Green Hill Care Home
Ticket went through a hole under the fence, clearly not for the first time, and sat down under one of the windows on the ground floor.
A minute later the window opened. An old woman looked out, and her whole face lit up.
"There you are," she said. She put her hand out through the window, and Ticket pushed his head up under it.
I stood at the gate and watched. They stayed like that for a long time. She talked to him quietly. He didn't move.
Later, a nurse told me the story. The woman, Mrs. Hall, had lived on Hill Road for forty years. When she moved into the care home in the spring, she couldn't bring her dog, so a neighbor took him in.
"He was fine for about a week," the nurse said. "Then one morning he was here, under her window. We still don't know how he found it."
"He takes the bus," I said.
The nurse looked at me like I was crazy.
The next morning at 7:15, Ticket got on my bus as usual. He walked past me and sat down by the window.
He never paid for a ticket. I never asked him to.

questions.question: Where did the dog get off every morning?
questions.explain: 아침 7시 15분에 힐 로드에서 타서 파크 스트리트에서 내렸다.

questions.question: Why did the student call the dog Ticket?
options: He sat by the ticket machine.
questions.explain: 표 없이 타는 개라서 '티켓'이라고 불렀다.

questions.question: How did the driver find out where the dog went?
options: He followed the dog on his day off.
He saw the dog from the bus window.
questions.explain: 쉬는 날 평상복을 입고 같은 버스를 타서 따라갔다.

questions.question: Who was the old woman at the window?
options: The dog's owner, who now lived in the care home
questions.explain: 홀 부인은 힐 로드에 40년 살다가 요양원에 들어갔고, 개는 데려갈 수 없어 이웃이 맡았다.

questions.question: "He never paid for a ticket. I never asked him to." What does the driver feel?
options: He is angry at the dog.
He is happy to let the dog ride free.
He wants the nurse to pay.
He plans to stop the dog next time.
questions.explain: 사연을 안 뒤로 기사는 티켓을 그냥 태워 준다. 묻지도 않는 것이 그의 마음이다.

questions.question: "So on my day off, I found out." What does out add?
options: The answer came out into the open after looking.
He found something he had lost.
questions.explain: out은 안에 감춰져 있던 것이 밖으로 드러나는 그림이다. find는 찾는 것, find out은 몰랐던 사실이 드러나 알게 되는 것이다.
questions.basis: 감각 사전 out(이미지: 안에 있던 것이 밖으로 드러남). find out은 사전 줄에 없고 보강 1(입자 감각)의 out 줄에 있음

questions.question: "He was fine for about a week." What does for show?
options: The week was a gift for him.
How long he was fine, from start to end.
questions.explain: 기간 for는 그 상태가 얼마나 이어졌는지 길이를 말하며, 이미지로 풀지 않고 덩어리로 익힌다. 어느 때인지를 말할 때는 during을 쓴다(보강 9.11, 9.15).
questions.basis: 보강 9.11(Mueller 2016의 잠정 추정과 학습자 사전의 따로 둔 뜻), 9.15(Cambridge Grammar의 for/during). 감각 사전 밖이고 모델 밖(가설)

paragraphs.text: Every evening at seven, Mr. Ortiz played the piano. He lived next door, in the blue house with the big window, and in summer he kept the window open. I used to hate it. I mean, who wants to hear the same slow song every night while they're doing homework? But after a few years, I was used to it. It was kind of like the sound of the dishwasher. You only notice it when it stops.
Then one night in October, it stopped.
"Did you hear that?" I asked Mom.
"Hear what?"
"Nothing. Mr. Ortiz didn't play."
"Maybe he's busy or something," she said.
He didn't play the next night, or the night after that. On Saturday my friend Sam came over, and I told him about it.
"So go knock on his door," Sam said.
"I can't just knock on his door. We've lived next to each other for ten years, and we've never really talked. He says hi. I say hi. That's it."
Sam looked at me for a second. "Okay. I'll come with you."
We stood in front of the blue door for a long time before I rang the bell. When Mr. Ortiz opened it, I could tell something was wrong. His right arm was in a white cast, up to his elbow.
"I fell on the ice outside the grocery store," he said. "Broken wrist. Six weeks."
"So you can't play," I said.

"Not with one hand. You know, I've played that song every night for thirty years. My wife used to sit right there, next to the window, and listen. After she died, I just kept playing. I guess it felt like she was still in the room."
Nobody said anything. Then all of a sudden Sam said, "He plays piano."
He was pointing at me.
"Sam!"
"What? You do. You had lessons."
"For two years. When I was eight."
Mr. Ortiz looked at me. "Do you remember any of it?"
"Some," I said. "Kind of."
That's how I ended up at Mr. Ortiz's piano that afternoon, with Mr. Ortiz on the bench next to me. He picked up an old music book, opened it to a page full of pencil marks, and put it in front of me.
"You don't have to play the whole thing," he said. "Just the right hand. I'll do the left."
We were terrible. I kept stopping. He kept laughing. Sam sat on the couch and ate all the cookies. Once he looked up and was like, "You two should start a band."
After that, I went over every afternoon. My other friends thought it was weird that I hung out with an old man after school. I didn't care. I have to say, it was the best part of my day.
The next Saturday at seven, I sat down next to him, and we played the song from beginning to end. It wasn't perfect, but it was the song.
When we finished, I heard clapping. I turned around. Outside the open window stood my mom, Sam, the lady from across the street, and two kids on bikes.
"We wondered where the music went," the lady said.
Mr. Ortiz looked up at me. His eyes were wet.
"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.
"Of course," I said.

questions.question: Why did the narrator notice something was wrong in October?
questions.explain: 매일 저녁 일곱 시에 들리던 피아노 소리가 그날 밤 들리지 않았다.

questions.question: Why couldn't Mr. Ortiz play the piano?
options: He broke his wrist on the ice.
questions.explain: 식료품점 앞 빙판에서 넘어져 손목이 부러졌고, 오른팔에 깁스를 했다.

questions.question: Why did Mr. Ortiz play the same song every night?
options: It was the only song he knew.
It made him feel like his wife was still there.
He was practicing for a concert.
questions.explain: 아내가 창가에 앉아 듣던 곡이라, 치고 있으면 아내가 아직 방에 있는 것 같았다.

questions.question: What did the people outside the window show at the end?
options: They were angry about the noise.
They had missed the music too.
They were waiting for the bus.
questions.explain: "음악이 어디 갔나 했다"는 말에서 이웃들도 그 노래를 기다리고 있었다는 것을 알 수 있다. 소리는 멈춰야 알아챈다는 첫 문단과 이어진다.

questions.question: "I used to hate it. ... But after a few years, I was used to it." What does the narrator mean?
options: 예전엔 싫었는데, 몇 년 지나자 익숙해졌다.
예전엔 좋았는데, 몇 년 지나자 싫어졌다.
questions.explain: used to + 동사원형은 '예전엔 ~했다', be used to + 명사는 '~에 익숙하다'다. 모양은 비슷해도 뜻이 다르다.

questions.question: "That's how I ended up at Mr. Ortiz's piano that afternoon." What does "ended up" show?
options: He planned it for a long time.
It happened in the end, after things he didn't plan.
questions.explain: end up은 계획하지 않은 일들을 거쳐 '결국 ~하게 되다'다. 샘이 갑자기 말을 꺼낸 탓에 피아노 앞에 앉게 됐다.

questions.question: "Once he looked up and was like, 'You two should start a band.'" What does "was like" do here?
options: It says Sam liked the band.
It reports what Sam said, in a casual way.
questions.explain: 구어에서 he was like, ...는 '걔가 막 ~하더라'처럼 남의 말이나 반응을 옮긴다. said보다 가볍고 생생하다.

paragraphs.text: My grandmother started school when she was seventy-four.

She grew up on a farm, and in her village the girls didn't get to go to school. They worked. "Every morning I watched my brothers walk away with their books," she told me once, "and I stood there with the chickens."
So when she saw a sign at the library, FREE READING CLASS FOR ADULTS, TUESDAYS 7 P.M., she signed up the same day, even though my dad thought it was a bad idea.
"Mom, it's at night. It's cold. What kind of school is open at night? Why don't you let me teach you at home?"
"You?" she said. "You can't even teach the dog to sit."
And that was that.
One Tuesday in January, Mom and Dad both had to work late, so I went with her.

The classroom was in the basement of the library. There were about twelve people, all adults, sitting at small tables. When we walked in, everyone stopped talking and stared at me. I guess they didn't see a lot of twelve-year-olds.
The teacher was a young man with a beard and a big smile. "Welcome back, Mrs. Rivera," he said. "And who's this?"
"My grandson. He's here to watch."
"Great. Why don't you take that seat by the window?" he said to me. "Okay, so, everybody. Tonight we're going to write a short letter."
People groaned. Grandma didn't. She took out her pencil.

I didn't know what kind of class it was going to be. I thought it would be boring, like my school. It wasn't. A man from Brazil read a sentence about his truck, and everybody clapped. A woman who worked at a hotel raised her hand five times to ask about the letter Q. When the teacher asked, "Who wants to read first?" Grandma raised her hand before he finished the question.
She read slowly. "The... sun... is... hot." Then she looked up, very proud.
"Perfect," the teacher said.
From the back, someone called out, "Go, Mrs. Rivera!"
On the way home, I said, "Grandma, you're the star of that class."
"No," she said. "Kim is the star. She can read a whole menu. I'm just the oldest."
"You're the loudest, too."
"You're right," she laughed. "That's what my mother always said."

After that, I went with her every Tuesday. I didn't have to, but I wanted to. I got to know all of them. Kim, who wanted to read to her baby. Marco, who wanted to pass his driving test. Old Mr. Patel, who just wanted to read the newspaper without asking his wife.
In May, the class had a small party. Everyone had to write one more letter and read it out loud.
"Mrs. Rivera!" the teacher called out. "You're next."
Grandma stood up and unfolded a piece of paper. Then she looked straight at me.
"Dear Daniel," she read. "Thank you for coming with me. You did not have to. Every Tuesday I get to go to school, and every Tuesday you are next to me. That is better than a book."
Everybody turned to look at me. This time I didn't mind being stared at.
Oh, by the way, she can read a whole menu now. She orders for me.

questions.question: Why didn't Grandma go to school as a child?
options: She lived too far from the school.
In her village, girls had to work instead.
questions.explain: 그 마을에서는 여자아이들이 학교에 가지 못하고 일했다.

questions.question: Why did Daniel go to the class the first time?
options: His parents both had to work late.
He wanted to learn to read.
questions.explain: 엄마와 아빠가 둘 다 늦게까지 일해야 해서 할머니를 따라갔다.

questions.question: How did Grandma act in class?
options: She was eager and raised her hand first.
questions.explain: 선생님이 질문을 다 끝내기도 전에 손을 들었고, 천천히 읽은 뒤 뿌듯해했다.

questions.question: Why didn't Daniel mind being stared at at the end?
options: Everyone was looking at him because of Grandma's kind letter.
He was wearing a funny hat.
He was reading his own letter.
questions.explain: 할머니가 편지에서 매주 곁에 있어 준 다니엘에게 고마워했기 때문이다. 처음 왔을 때 빤히 쳐다보던 장면과 짝을 이룬다.

questions.question: "In her village the girls didn't get to go to school." What does "didn't get to" mean?
questions.explain: get to + 동사는 '~할 수 있게 되다, ~할 기회를 얻다'다. 끝의 'Every Tuesday I get to go to school'은 그 기회를 이제야 누린다는 기쁨이다.

questions.question: "Why don't you take that seat by the window?" What is the teacher doing?
questions.explain: Why don't you ~?는 이유를 묻는 말이 아니라 '~하는 게 어때?' 하는 부드러운 제안이다.

questions.question: "When we walked in, everyone stopped talking and stared at me." How is "stared at" different from "looked at"?
options: They looked for a long time without looking away.
They looked but didn't see him.
questions.explain: stare at은 눈길을 한 점에 박고 떼지 않는 것이다. look at보다 오래 머물러서 받는 사람은 불편하다.

paragraphs.text: I have always been the kid whose parents drive her everywhere. Piano lessons, the dentist, Ruby's house, which is four blocks away. Everybody my age in this city takes the subway by themselves. I've never taken it alone. Not once.
So when high school started, I made a speech at dinner.
"I'm fifteen," I said. "On the first day of school, I'm taking the subway. Alone. I hate being the only one whose dad drops her off."
My mom looked at my dad. My dad looked at his soup.
"Okay," Mom said finally.
I was ready for a fight. I didn't get one. That should have been my first clue.

On the first day, I left the house at 7:15. The moment I went down the stairs into the station, my heart started racing. It was so loud. There were so many people. I held my card like it was made of gold.
The train came, and I got on and found a seat. I was doing it. I was really doing it.
Then I saw her.

At the other end of the car, there was a woman in a huge yellow hat and big black sunglasses, holding a newspaper in front of her face. Who reads a newspaper on the subway? Nobody. Nobody except a parent who is trying to hide.
My phone buzzed. It was Ruby.
What's up? Are you on the train?
Yes,
I wrote.
And I think my mom is following me.
No way.
Yellow hat. Newspaper.
I hate that I'm missing this.
I got off at my stop. So did the yellow hat. I walked up the stairs. So did the yellow hat. At the top I stopped, turned around, and said, "Mom. Seriously?"
The newspaper came down slowly.
It wasn't my mom.
It was my dad. In my mom's hat.
"She said I'd look less suspicious," he said.
My dad has always been terrible at hiding things. Every Christmas he hides the presents in the same closet.
I don't remember the last time I laughed that hard. People were staring at us. Dad was laughing too, and the hat blew off, and he had to chase it down the sidewalk. I've never seen him run so fast.
"Go," he said finally. "Go to school. I'll go back home. I promise."
"You'd better."

The day was fine. Better than fine. I found all my classes. I ate lunch with Ruby and a girl named Tess from my art class, and the three of us made fun of the cafeteria pizza. When I told them about the hat, Tess almost fell off her chair.
After school I took the subway home by myself. No hat. No newspaper. I checked.
At dinner I said, "Tomorrow, when I go back to school, I'm going alone. For real this time."
"Of course," said Mom.
"Of course," said Dad.
The next morning I got on the train, found a seat, and looked around carefully. Nothing. I relaxed.
Then I noticed the old man across from me. He was wearing a big coat and reading a book.
The book was upside down.
"Grandpa?"

questions.question: What did the narrator want to do on the first day of high school?
options: Get a ride from her dad.
questions.explain: 늘 부모님이 데려다줬는데, 첫날은 혼자 지하철을 타겠다고 선언했다.

questions.question: Why did she think the woman in the yellow hat was her mom?
options: She was hiding behind a newspaper.
She was wearing her mom's coat.
questions.explain: 요즘 지하철에서 신문을 읽는 사람은 없으니, 숨으려는 부모라고 생각했다.

questions.question: Who was really under the yellow hat?
questions.explain: 엄마 모자를 쓴 아빠였다. 엄마가 그러면 덜 수상해 보일 거라고 했다.

questions.question: What does the ending suggest?
options: Her grandpa was now secretly following her.
questions.explain: 책을 거꾸로 들고 있는 노인은 할아버지였다. 이번엔 할아버지가 몰래 따라온 것이다.

questions.question: "The moment I went down the stairs into the station, my heart started racing." What does "the moment" mean here?
questions.explain: the moment + 문장은 '~하자마자, ~하는 바로 그때'다. 계단을 내려가자마자 가슴이 뛰기 시작했다.

questions.question: "I've never taken it alone. Not once." What does she mean?
options: She has not taken it alone even one time.
She doesn't like taking it alone.
questions.explain: I've never + 과거분사는 '한 번도 ~한 적 없다'다. 뒤의 Not once가 그 뜻을 다시 굳힌다.

questions.question: Ruby texts, "What's up? Are you on the train?" What does "What's up?" mean here?
questions.explain: what's up은 '무슨 일이야?, 잘 돼 가?'라는 가벼운 인사이자 물음이다.

paragraphs.text: I've been friends with Chloe since we were five. We sit with each other on the bus. We sit with each other at lunch. We talk on the phone every night, even though we just saw each other an hour ago. My dad says we talk so much that our phones need a vacation.
So when Chloe didn't save me a seat on the bus on Monday, I thought it was a mistake.
It wasn't. On Monday she sat with Grace. At lunch she sat with the soccer girls. When I said hi in the hallway, she looked at the floor and kept walking.
"Is Chloe mad at you?" my brother asked at dinner.
"I don't know," I said. "She won't talk to me."
"What did you do?"
"Nothing!"
I kept thinking about it all night. Did I forget her birthday? No, that's in March. Did I say something about her new haircut? I liked her new haircut. I couldn't think of anything.
On Tuesday I kept trying. I waited by her locker. I sent her a funny video of a goat. She didn't answer. On Wednesday I sat down at her lunch table, and she picked up her tray and moved.
That one hurt a lot.
On Thursday I went to her house after school. Her mom opened the door and smiled at me, the same way she always does. "She's in her room, honey. Go on up."
Chloe was on her bed, reading. When she saw me, she turned to the wall.
"You want to tell me why you're mad at me?" I said. "Because I really don't know."
For a long time she didn't say anything. Then she said, very quietly, "When were you going to tell me?"
"Tell you what?"

"That you're moving. I heard your mom talking to my mom on Sunday. 'She's leaving in June,' she said. 'I'm going to miss her so much.'" Chloe's eyes were red. "So you're just going to leave? And you didn't even talk about it with me?"
I stared at her. Then I started to laugh. I couldn't stop.
"It's not funny!" she said.
"Chloe. My mom was talking about my sister. Emma's going to college in June."
Chloe sat up. "Your sister?"
"My sister. In California. Mom talks about it a lot. She cries about it a lot, too, even though Emma says she'll come back every Christmas."
"You're not moving?"
"I'm not going anywhere. You're stuck with me."
Chloe put her face in her pillow and made a long noise. "I've been so mean to you all week."
"Yeah, you have. The goat video was really good, by the way."
"I watched it eleven times," she said.
The next morning, my seat on the bus was waiting for me. Chloe had her bag on it so nobody else could take it.
We talked about everything all the way to school. Then, just before we got off, she grabbed my arm.
"Promise me something," she said. "If you ever do move away, you'll come back."
"I promise."
"And you'll talk to me first. Not your mom. Me."
"Deal," I said. "You want to sit with me at lunch?"
She rolled her eyes. "Obviously. I want to be friends with you until we're a hundred."

paragraphs.text: Every Friday, our school paper has a column called "Ask Dude." Kids put letters in a box outside the library, and Dude answers them. How to talk to your crush. What to do when your little brother reads your diary. How to survive a group project and stuff.
Nobody knows who Dude is. People have guesses. Some think it's a teacher. Some think it's an eighth grader with a beard.
It's me. I'm in sixth grade, and I don't even have a mustache.

Only Ms. Grant, who runs the paper, knows. She asked me in September because, she said, "You give good advice, and you don't talk too much." I said yes as soon as she finished the sentence. I hope she never finds out the second part isn't true.

The hard part is keeping it a secret from Marcus. Marcus is my best friend. We've walked home together almost every day since second grade. But Dude's answers are due on Thursdays at 3:30, so every Thursday, as soon as the bell rang, I ran out the door. I never told him why.
Then one Thursday, I opened the box and found this:
Dear Dude,

My best friend has been acting weird for a month. Every Thursday he runs away from me after school. He doesn't even say bye. When I ask him what's wrong, he says he's busy with homework and stuff. I think he has a new best friend. What should I do?
Left Behind
I read it three times. I knew that handwriting. Marcus makes his g's look like little snails.
I felt terrible. I wanted to tell him about everything right then. But I couldn't, not without telling him I was Dude.
So I did the only thing I could do. I answered the letter.
Dear Left Behind,

Let me tell you something: your friend does not have a new best friend. I'm sure about this. He's probably doing something he's embarrassed about. Maybe he's taking dance lessons. Maybe he's writing poems. Give him a little time. He still thinks you're the best. At least, I hope he does.
Dude
On Friday, the paper came out. At lunch, Marcus read the column with his face very close to the page. He didn't say anything. He didn't even look up.
After school we walked home together. Halfway there, he stopped.
"So," he said. "Dance lessons?"
"What?"
"Are you taking dance lessons?"
I looked at him. He looked at me.
"Marcus, I..."
"Dude," he said, and he started laughing. "
Dude.
"How did you know?"
"I remember the first column. In September. Dude said a group project is 'like a sandwich nobody wants to make.' You said that exact thing to me in fourth grade. I knew right away."
"Then why did you write the letter?"
"I wanted to see what you'd say." He grinned. "Also, you really did run away from me every Thursday. That part was true."
"I'm sorry," I said. And I was.
"It's fine. At least now I know you're not taking dance lessons." He started walking again. "But I have one condition."
"What?"
"Next week," Marcus said, "let me pick the letters."

paragraphs.text: Nora's family is going away for a week, and I'm the one who has to take care of her fish.
"His name is Bubbles," she says. She hands me a box of fish food and a long list. "One pinch in the morning. One pinch at night. Not more."
"It's a fish," I say. "It's not a big deal."
She looks at me as if I just said something terrible. "It's a big deal to me."
Nora lives next door, and I know she's serious. I promise to take care of him. At the door, her dad shakes my hand, as if I'm taking care of their whole house and not one small goldfish.
"Good luck," says Nora's little brother. He says it like he knows something I don't.
The first day goes fine. One pinch of food. Easy.
On the second morning, Bubbles is floating at the top of the water.
I look down at him for a long time. I tap the glass. Nothing.
"Mom," I call. "I think I killed Nora's fish."
Mom comes in, looks at the bowl, and shakes her head. "Did you give him too much food?"
"One pinch!" I say. "I followed the list!"
"Fish die sometimes," she says. "It's not your fault."
But I know Nora. She won't be okay with "sometimes."

So after school I ride my bike to the pet store. There are lots of goldfish there. Lots and lots of them. I look at every single one. Finally I find one that looks just like Bubbles: orange, with a little white spot on his tail.
"Good luck with him," the man at the store says, and I don't ask what he means.
For the rest of the week, I take care of the new Bubbles like he's made of glass. One pinch in the morning. One pinch at night. I talk to him. I tell him to act natural.
On Sunday, Nora's family comes home. It's her birthday, so Mom and I bring over a cake. Nora goes straight to her room to see Bubbles. I follow her. My heart is beating very fast.
She looks down at the bowl. She doesn't say anything for a while.
"He looks good," she says.
"He was great," I say. "No problems at all." I try to look relaxed. I pretend to be very interested in her bookshelf.
She nods slowly. Then she turns around. "You know that's not Bubbles, right?"
My face gets hot. I open my mouth, but she shakes her head.
"It's okay," she says. "The one I left with you wasn't Bubbles either. He was Bubbles Number Three."
"What?"
"The first one died when I was eight. Mom keeps buying new ones. She thinks I don't notice." She smiles a little. "I pretend not to. It makes her happy."
"So you're okay with it?" I say.
"I'm okay with it," she says. "But you're really bad at pretending. That's kind of nice."
In the kitchen, they light the candles. Nora closes her eyes for a long time before she blows them out.
"Did you make a wish?" I ask her later.
"Yes," she says. "I wished for a fish that lives longer than a week."
"That's not funny," I say. But I laugh anyway.

paragraphs.text: The first night, I thought it was a dream.
I was in bed, almost asleep, when I heard music. It was very quiet, and it was coming from downstairs. Then I heard a bump, and someone said, "Ow."
In the morning I asked about it at breakfast.
"Music?" said Mom. "I didn't hear any music."
"I don't know what you heard, sweetie," said Dad. "Maybe it was the neighbors."
"It wasn't the neighbors," I said. "It was in our kitchen."
"I don't know," said Dad again, and he got up to wash his plate. Dad never washes his plate.

The next night I stayed awake on purpose. I lay in the dark with my eyes open. At first there was nothing. Then, at about eleven, I could hear it again: soft music, and the sound of feet. Step, step, slide. Step, step, slide. Bump. "Ow."
In the morning I asked my little brother Max, "Did you hear the music last night?"
"What music?" said Max. Max could sleep through a fire truck.

On the third night I got up. I walked down the stairs very slowly, and I didn't turn on any lights. The kitchen door was open a little. I could see Dad's phone on the table. On the screen, a man and a woman were dancing.
And in the middle of the kitchen, in his pajamas, was Dad. He was dancing with a broom.
Step, step, slide. He turned and hit the table with his knee. "Ow," he said quietly.
I put my hand over my mouth so I wouldn't laugh, and I went back up to bed. But I couldn't go to sleep for a long time. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw Dad and the broom.
Ten days later, it was Mom and Dad's anniversary. After dessert, Dad got up and put on some music. It was the song from the kitchen.
"Would you like to dance?" he said to Mom.
"Oh my God," said Mom. "You don't dance."
"I do now," said Dad.

At first Mom just laughed. Then she took his hand, and they danced, right there in the living room. Step, step, slide. Dad didn't hit anything. He didn't say "ow" once. Max and I clapped. Then Grandma, who was visiting, just started crying into her napkin.
"Why are you crying?" Max asked her.
"I don't know," said Grandma. "It's the sweetest thing in the world."
That night Mom came to say good night. She sat on my bed.
"I love you," she said.
"I love you too," I said. Then I asked, "Were you surprised?"
Mom smiled. "Can you keep a secret?"
I nodded.

"I could hear him every night," she said. "Step, step, slide. Bump. Ow. Our bedroom is right above the kitchen." She kissed my head. "Your dad is the best man in the world. But he's terrible at secrets."
"So that's why you said you didn't hear any music."
"That's why," said Mom. "Now go to sleep."

paragraphs.text: When I was little, my brother Sam was too old to play with me. He was six years older and always busy. Then one day, he took a coin out of my ear, and I screamed so loud that Mom ran in from the kitchen.

After that, I followed him everywhere. "Show me another one," I said, every day. Sam was such a show-off that he always said yes. He showed me a few tricks. Then a few more. I grew up with a deck of cards in my pocket.

Last fall, Sam went away to college. It's six hours by car. I didn't think I would miss him so much. I missed him more than summer, more than our old dog. The house was too quiet. No one took coins out of my ears.

We talked on the phone a few times a week. I told him about the school talent show. I was going to do a card trick, the big one he taught me before he left. I don't know why I didn't tell him I was scared.
"You need a volunteer from the audience," he said. "Someone to pick a card. Just don't pick Mom. She always tells everyone the card."
On the night of the show, I was a mess. My hands were cold. I had my cards in my pocket and my lucky hat on my head. Mr. Ortiz, the music teacher, was backstage with a list.
"Ben, you're next," he said. "Are you okay?"
"I can't go on," I said.
"Last-minute nerves," he said. "Everyone gets them. Take a deep breath."
I took a deep breath. It didn't help. But the girl before me finished her song, and Mr. Ortiz gave me a little push, and I walked out on the stage.
The lights were very bright. I couldn't see any faces, only shapes. I took off my hat, the way Sam always did, and held up the cards.
"I need a volunteer," I said.
No one moved. It was so quiet I could hear a chair move. I was going to run off the stage. I really was. My feet were already turning.
Then one hand went up, in the very last row.
"Okay," I said. "You. In the back."
He walked down the middle of the room. Tall. A big coat. A hat pulled down low. I don't know why, but my heart started beating faster.
He stopped in front of the stage and took off his hat.
It was Sam.
"What's going on?" I said, right into the microphone. Everyone laughed.
"Last-minute bus ticket," said Sam. "Six hours. Pick a card, right?"
He picked a card. He showed it to the audience but not to me. I mixed the cards, just like he taught me, and I found it on the first try. The seven of hearts. Everyone clapped, really clapped.
After the show, Sam put his arm around me.
"You didn't need me up there," he said. "You know that, right?"
"I know," I said.
That was a lie, and he knew it. He let me tell it anyway. Then he reached over and took a coin out of my ear.
It was such a stupid trick. I loved it more than ever.

paragraphs.text: In middle school, everyone is known for something. Jake is known for his jokes. Priya is known for her drawings. Leo is known for eating a worm in fourth grade, and he will be known for that forever.
I'm not known for anything. I'm just Maya, third row, by the window.
Owen is known for not talking. In two months, I think I've heard him say ten words.
Our class has a hamster named Pickles. Every Friday, someone takes him home for the weekend. Last Friday it was Owen's turn.
On Monday morning, Ms. Lee walked in and stopped in front of the shelf. The cage was there. The little door was open. Pickles was not.
"Okay, everyone, take your seats," she said. "Owen. What happened to Pickles?"
Everyone turned around. Owen's face went red.
"I don't know," he said quietly. "I put the cage on the shelf before the bell. When I got back from my locker, the door was open."
"No way," said Jake. "He lost Pickles!"
Some kids started to laugh. Somebody said, "Maybe he ate him." More kids laughed.
Owen looked down at his desk. His hands were shaking.
Then I did something I never do. I stood up.
"Hey," I said. "Stop it. You guys don't know what happened. Pickles opened that door before. Remember? Twice."
It was true. Pickles was good at doors.
The room got quiet. Jake put his hands in the air, like, okay, okay. I sat down very fast. My heart was going crazy. I'm not someone who stands up for people. I'm not someone who stands up at all.
Ms. Lee pointed at the sign over the board. It said BE KIND in big blue letters.
"Maya's right," she said. "Let's be kind. And let's look for him. He can't be far."
So we looked for Pickles. We looked under the desks and behind the books. Owen went to look for him in the hallway with Mr. Diaz, the janitor. No Pickles.
At lunch, Owen sat down across from me. He didn't say anything. He just gave me half of his cookie. I think that was his way of saying thank you.
When we got back to the classroom after lunch, Ms. Lee was standing very still by the supply closet.
"You guys," she whispered. "Come here. Quietly."
On the bottom shelf of the closet, in a box of old paper, was Pickles. And next to Pickles were five tiny pink babies.
"Oh," said Priya.
"Pickles is a girl?" said Jake.

The whole class started to laugh again, but it was a different kind of laugh this time. Owen looked at me, and I looked at him, and he put his hand up. I gave him a high-five. Then Jake high-fived him too, and then everyone did.
"Okay, take your seats," said Ms. Lee, smiling. "Pickles needs some quiet."
Ms. Lee let Owen name the babies, because he took care of Pickles all weekend. The last one was the smallest, with a white spot on its nose.
"Maya," he said.
So now I'm known for something. I'm the girl with a hamster named after her.

questions.question: What is Owen known for?

paragraphs.text: At 6:30, Mia's radio came on. A happy voice said, "Good morning, everybody! It's Tuesday, and it's gonna be a cold one. It's cold out there, so wear a hat!"
Mia sat up in bed. She knew those words. She had heard them yesterday.
"No way," she said.
She walked to work at the little café on Main Street. At 7:00, Mr. Bell came in with his brown dog. He ordered a large coffee, turned around, and knocked it over. Just like yesterday.
At 7:30, a woman in a red hat came to the counter. "Excuse me," she said. "Is the bus to the city late again?"
Mia's hands began to shake. The same woman. The same hat. The same question.
She pulled her coworker Sam into the kitchen. "Sam, I think it's the same day."
Sam was washing cups. "What?"
"Yesterday was Tuesday. Today is Tuesday. What's going on?"
Sam looked at her for a long moment. Then he laughed.
"Come on, Mia. Let me guess. The radio said it's gonna be cold."
"Yes!"
"That show isn't live. The DJ is on vacation, so they play the same tape every day this week. And Mr. Bell spilled his coffee, right?"
"Yes."
"He spills it every day. You know that. Am I right?"
Mia thought about it. "Okay. But the woman in the red hat..."
"She asks about the bus every morning. And every morning it's late. It's kind of her hobby."
Mia sat down on a box of milk. "So it's not the same day?"
"I don't think so," Sam said. "It's a small town, you know. Every day looks the same here."
"I thought I was going crazy."
"You're not crazy. You're bored. That's different."
That night, Mia couldn't sleep. Same radio. Same coffee. Same bus. She didn't want to live the same day for the rest of her life.
On Wednesday, at 7:00, Mr. Bell came in. He took his coffee and started to turn around. This time Mia was ready. She reached over the counter and caught the cup.
Mr. Bell looked down at his dry shoes. "Well," he said. "That's new."
"Would you like a lid with that?" Mia asked.
At 7:30, the woman in the red hat came in. "Excuse me. Is the bus late again?"
"Yes," Mia said. "But you don't have to wait for it. I finish at eight, and I gotta go to the city anyway. Let's go together. I can drive you."
The woman smiled. "Oh, I don't want to go to the city."
"You don't?"
"No. I've never wanted to go. I just like asking. It's the only time anyone talks to me all day."
Mia didn't know what to say. Then she pulled out a chair.
"All right," she said. "Then sit down. What do you want to talk about?"
The woman thought for a moment. "I don't know," she said. "Nobody has asked me that in years."
Sam came out of the kitchen with three cups. "Come on, you two. Hot chocolate is on me."
Outside, the bus came and went. Nobody got on.
It was a cold Wednesday, and it was not like any other day.

paragraphs.text: Grandma's apple pie was gone.
At three o'clock it was cooling on the kitchen window. At three-fifteen, there was only an empty plate.
Lily was eleven, and she wanted to be a police officer more than anything.
"I'll take the case," she said.
Her little brother Max laughed. "It's just a pie."
"It's not just a pie. It's a crime. Shut up and get my notebook."
Lily looked at the window. Then she looked at the ground under it. There were small footprints in the mud.
"Look at this," she said. "Someone was standing right here. Someone with feet a little smaller than mine."
"Like who?" Max asked.
"I don't know yet. But I'm gonna find out. Come on, Max. We gotta find the thief before dinner."

The first suspect was Tom from next door. Tom was twelve and had a lemonade stand. His sign said MAGIC LEMONADE: MAKES YOU SMARTER. ONE DOLLAR. When they got there, he was trying to sell a cup to a man on a bike.
"Did you take my grandma's pie?" Lily asked.
"What pie? I've been here all day," Tom said. "Do you want to buy some magic lemonade?"
Lily tried a cup. "This is just water with sugar."
"It's called a hustle," Tom said. "Look at my money box. It works. And you know what? For one more dollar, I'll tell you what I saw today."
Lily paid. Tom leaned close. "I saw nothing."
Lily wrote in her notebook: Tom. No crumbs. Not him.
The second suspect was the big white dog across the street. It was asleep in the sun, and its face was clean.
"Do you think it was the dog?" Lily asked.
"I think the dog's too fat to jump that high," Max said.
"That's kind of mean," Lily said. "But you're right."
Back home, Lily sat on the steps and closed her notebook. She felt a little stupid.
"A real cop always cracks the case," she said. "I'm never gonna be a real cop."
"Come on," Max said. "You're really good at this. You have to keep going."
Lily looked at him. Then she looked at his shoes. They were small and muddy.
"Max," she said slowly. "Why are your shoes muddy?"
Max's face went red.
"And what is that on your shirt?"
He looked down. A small piece of apple was stuck to it.
"Okay, okay! I took it," Max said. "But I didn't eat it! It's under my bed. I was gonna give it back."
"What do you mean? Why did you take it?"
Max looked at his feet. "You were sad all week. You kept saying nothing ever happens here. I was just trying to help. You know, I wanted to give you a real case."
Lily was quiet for a moment.
"Let me get this straight," she said. "You stole a pie... for me?"
"Yeah."
"That's the worst crime I've ever heard of," Lily said. Then she hugged him.
Grandma got the pie out from under Max's bed.
"All right, detectives," she said, and cut three big pieces. "Case closed?"
"Not yet," Lily said. She opened her notebook and wrote one more line.
Max. Took the pie. Reason: good.
"Now it's closed," she said. "Got it?"
"Got it," said Max, and took the biggest piece.

paragraphs.text: "Noah. Noah, wake up."
Noah opened one eye. His dad was standing next to the bed with a flashlight.
"What's going on?" Noah said. "It's the middle of the night."
"It's three in the morning. Come on, get dressed. We gotta leave now. We're gonna see shooting stars."
Noah wanted to say no. But his dad looked so excited. Noah got up.
They drove out of town in the old blue car. Dad talked the whole way.
"When I was your age, my dad used to wake me up just like this," he said. "Once a year. We went to the same hill every time. You're gonna love it."
"I know, Dad. You told me."
"I did?"
"Like ten times," Noah said. "But you know, it's okay. Tell me again."
Dad laughed and told him again.
After forty minutes, the road turned into a dirt road. The dirt road turned into mud. Then the car stopped moving.
Dad pressed the gas. The wheels turned and turned, and mud flew everywhere.
"Hold on," Dad said. "Hold on. I've got this."
He didn't have it.
Noah looked at his phone. No signal. "Dad, we got stuck. And I think we're lost."
"We're not lost. Look, the hill is right there." Dad pointed into the dark. "We just have to walk a little. Let's go."
"A little" was thirty minutes, uphill, in the cold. Noah's shoes got wet. His hands got cold. He slipped and fell in the mud.
"Are you all right?" Dad asked. "Come on, give me your hand."
"I'm fine." He wasn't. "This was supposed to be fun."
"It's gonna be fun. Wait till we get to the top."
They got to the top. Dad looked up. Noah looked up.
The sky was full of clouds. Not one star.
For a long time, neither of them said anything.
"Well," Dad said quietly. "That's kind of funny."
"It's not funny," Noah said. "My feet are wet. The car is stuck. And we can't see anything. Why did you even want to come here?"
Dad sat down on a rock. He didn't answer right away.
"You know, your grandpa and I came here every year," he said. "Then I got older and got busy, and we stopped. I always thought we'd go back one more time. Then he got sick, and we never did."
Noah sat down next to him.
"I don't know," Dad said. "I guess I wanted to do it right this time. I just wanted you to be happy up here, like I was."
Noah pulled his jacket closer. "I get it, Dad. It's okay."

They ate the cookies from Dad's pocket. Dad told stories about Grandpa: the time he fell into the lake, the time he sang to a cow. Noah laughed so hard he almost fell off the rock. It made him feel warm, even with wet feet.
At six, the sky started to get light. They walked back down, and a farmer pulled the car out of the mud with his tractor.
On the drive home, Noah looked out the window.
"Can we come back next year?" he asked.
Dad looked at him. "You want to come back? We didn't see a single star."
"Of course," Noah said. "But next year, let's check the weather first."

paragraphs.text: On her first morning at Blue Door Books, Kate got an e-mail at 7:00.
Good morning! Don't sit in the gray chair by the window. It's broken. (R)
Kate was alone in the office. She looked at the gray chair and sat in a different one.
At 9:00, her new boss, Mr. Grant, hurried in with a coffee in each hand.
"Kate! How's it going? First day, right?"
"Yes. It's going great," Kate said. "Um, who is R?"
"R?" Mr. Grant was already walking away. "Sorry, I've got a meeting. Let's talk later."
Just then, a man from sales sat down in the gray chair by the window. It broke, and he fell on the floor.
"Oh, my God," Kate said. "Are you all right?"
"I'm fine," he said from the floor. "I think we should get a new chair."
The next morning, at 7:00, there was another e-mail.
Mr. Grant is gonna ask you for the sales report. It's in the green folder, not the blue one. (R)
At 10:00, Mr. Grant came to her desk. "Kate, can you find the sales report? I think it's in the blue folder."
Kate handed him the green folder. He stared at her. "Wow. You're good. You know, you don't have to stay late tonight. Go home."
Every morning there was a new e-mail. Bring an umbrella. The coffee machine on the second floor is better. Be nice to Linda in accounting. She's a little scary, but she knows everything.
Kate tried to find out who R was. Nobody knew. She started to feel like someone was watching her.
On Friday, she went to Linda in accounting.
"I'm sorry to bother you," Kate said. "I mean, I know you're busy. But someone keeps e-mailing me. They know a lot about this office. Do you know anyone whose name starts with R?"
Linda took off her glasses. "Come on in. Do you want to sit down? Not in the gray chair."
"Let me take a look at those e-mails," Linda said. She read them, and she smiled a little.
"That's Rosa," she said. "She had your job before you. She retired last month after thirty years."
"But how does she know what's going to happen?"

"She doesn't. She just knows this office. The same things happen every week." Linda gave Kate her phone back. "Before she left, she wrote a lot of e-mails and set them to go out one by one. She said, 'I don't want the new person to feel lost like I did.'"
Kate read the e-mails again. "I want to thank her. Do you have her number?"
"I do. And you know what? She's gonna love that you asked." Linda wrote it down. "But hold on. You should read Monday's e-mail first."
"How do you know about Monday's e-mail?"
"Oh, I helped her write them," Linda said. "I get it. It's kind of strange. I mean, who does that? But that was Rosa."
On Monday at 7:00, the e-mail came.
This is the last one. You don't need me anymore. Now it's your turn. Write some for the next person. (R)
Kate laughed. Then she opened a new e-mail and began to type.
Good morning! Don't sit in the gray chair by the window. They still haven't fixed it.
